q: Why is procurement not a separate performance domain in the PMBOK Guide, Eighth Edition?
options: Procurement work is now covered entirely inside the Finance performance domain
They usually run through the organization's procurement department
Most projects today no longer buy any goods or services from outside sellers
PMI moved all of its procurement guidance into the Agile Practice Guide
explanation: Project procurements are usually integrated into, or extend from, the organization's procurement department, using its processes, policies and vendor relationships. Large projects may still have their own procurement team.

q: The PMBOK Guide says the buyer-seller relationship has a feature that is a source of several risks. Which one?
options: Shared ownership of all of the project's deliverables
A single accounting system for both parties
Equal access to every detail of the deal
Information asymmetry between the two parties
explanation: Each party may have different information about the transaction. This information asymmetry is a source of multiple relevant risks.

q: During Plan Sourcing Strategy, the team concludes that a common payroll module is cheaper to buy than to build. Which technique produced this conclusion?
options: Make-or-buy analysis
Source selection analysis
Bidder conference
Claims administration
explanation: A make-or-buy analysis compares buying with making internally and results in a decision on whether the team does the work or it is purchased. Source selection analysis chooses among sellers once the decision to buy is made.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Make-or-buy analysis and decisions

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Make-or-buy analysis and decisions

q: According to Table 2-3, which is an advantage of insourcing (make) over outsourcing (buy)?
options: It transfers delivery risk to the supplier
It frees capacity for the core strengths
It increases control over the deliverables
It is usually cheaper when the goods are common
explanation: Insourcing increases control and oversight of deliverables. Transferring delivery risk, freeing capacity and lower cost for common goods are advantages of outsourcing.

q: A new feature needs substantial innovation and is closely tied to the organization's competitive advantage. What does Table 2-3 suggest?
options: Make it: insourcing suits substantial new innovation
Outsource it, because external sellers always innovate faster
Outsource it, because that moves all strategic risk away
Use a sole-source contract with the most innovative vendor
explanation: Insourcing is often less expensive when substantial new innovation is required, and it gives tighter integration with the strategic advantage. Outsourcing is often cheaper for common goods or services.

q: Before sending bid documents to selected vendors, a buyer wants to learn what solutions the market offers. Which document should it use?
options: Request for quote
Invitation to tender (ITT)
Request for information
Request for proposal
explanation: An RFI gathers more information from the market before bid documents go out to a set of selected vendors.

q: The scope is complex, and the buyer wants each vendor to propose how it would solve the problem. Which bid document fits?
options: Request for quote
Request for proposal
Request for information
Purchase order
explanation: An RFP is used for a complex or complicated scope where the buyer is looking for the vendor to provide a solution.

q: The buyer needs 500 laptops of a known standard model, and price will decide the award. Which bid document fits?
options: Request for proposal
Request for information
Memorandum of agreement
Request for quote
explanation: An RFQ is used when price is the main deciding factor and the proposed solution is readily available.

q: After the bid documents go out, several bidders send questions about the scope. What should the buyer do?
options: Answer privately only the bidder most likely to win the work
Ignore the questions so that no bidder gains an advantage
Hold a bidder conference to answer every bidder's questions
Let each bidder change the statement of work as needed
explanation: The buyer generally holds a bidder conference to respond to questions and give clarifying information. The process must be transparent and fair, with equal opportunity for all sellers.

q: Why is it good practice to include the evaluation method in the bid documents?
options: So bidders know how they will be evaluated
So the buyer can change the method after bids arrive
So the cheapest bid is always selected automatically
So the legal review of the contract can be skipped
explanation: Competitive selection can make sellers invest much time up front. Telling them how they will be evaluated is transparent and builds stakeholder trust in the selection method.

q: A buyer is procuring routine office cleaning, with well-established standards and a well-defined outcome. Which selection method fits best?
options: Quality-based selection
Fixed budget
Single source
Least cost
explanation: Least cost suits standard or routine procurements with established practices and a well-defined outcome. For complex procurements it should be avoided, as it may hurt quality.

q: Only one supplier holds the patent for a component the project needs. Which selection method applies?
options: Single source
Least cost
Fixed budget
Qualifications only
explanation: Single source is a formal process used when only one supplier can meet the technical requirements, for example because of patents or exclusive rights. It is not a way to favor a provider.

q: When is the fixed-budget selection method appropriate?
options: When the scope is expected to change often during the work
When the buyer wants vendors to propose the budget
When the SOW is precise and no changes are expected
When only one supplier can meet the requirements
explanation: The budget is disclosed and the best proposal within it wins. Sellers adapt scope and quality to the budget, so the method fits only a precise SOW, no expected changes and a budget that cannot be exceeded.

q: A building's scope is fully defined and few changes are expected. Which contract type puts the cost risk mainly on the seller?
options: Cost plus fixed fee
Firm fixed price
Time and materials
Cost plus award fee
explanation: A fixed-price contract sets a fee for a clearly defined scope and transfers cost risk to the seller. The buyer gets budget certainty, but may pay a risk premium.

q: A research project's scope is uncertain and the work is high risk. Which contract type does the PMBOK Guide associate with this situation?
options: Firm fixed price
Fixed price with economic price adjustment
Fixed price incentive fee
Cost-reimbursable
explanation: Cost-reimbursable contracts pay actual costs plus a fee and are used when the scope is uncertain or the project is high risk, such as research and development.

q: The team needs two outside experts at once, and the work cannot be described in detail yet. Which contract type fits?
options: Time and materials
Firm fixed price with a detailed SOW
Fixed price incentive fee
Build-own-operate-transfer
explanation: T&M contracts are a hybrid, used for staff augmentation, outside experts, and when a precise statement of work cannot be written quickly. The buyer must monitor them closely to control costs.

q: A five-year supply contract is paid in a foreign currency, and the seller fears rising prices. Which contract type addresses this?
options: Cost plus award fee, judged by the buyer
Firm fixed price
Fixed price with economic price adjustment
Time and materials with a monthly rate review
explanation: FPEPA is used when the performance period spans years or payments are in another currency. It allows predefined adjustments for changed conditions, such as inflation or commodity prices.

q: Under a cost plus incentive fee contract, the final cost comes in below the target cost. What happens?
options: The seller keeps every dollar of savings as extra profit
Buyer and seller share the savings by a set formula
The buyer keeps all savings and cuts the fee
The contract converts to firm fixed price
explanation: In a CPIF contract, departures from the target cost are shared by a prenegotiated formula, for example an 80/20 split, based on the seller's actual performance.

q: An agile customer must cap total spending, but wants to add new ideas by replacing planned work. Which contract technique fits?
options: Not-to-exceed time and materials
Firm fixed price for the whole scope
Cost plus percentage of costs
A single all-in-one contract document
explanation: Not-to-exceed T&M limits the overall budget. New ideas can be added, but the customer manages to a given capacity, replacing original work with new work.
ref: Agile Practice Guide, Agile Procurement and Contracts

links.label: Agile Practice Guide, Agile Procurement and Contracts

q: Half the scope is done and the customer already has enough value. Which agile contract option lets the customer stop and pay a fee?
options: Dynamic scope option
Graduated time and materials
Early cancellation option
Multitiered structure
explanation: An early cancellation option lets the customer buy the remainder of the project for a cancellation fee. The customer limits budget exposure, and the supplier still earns revenue.
ref: Agile Practice Guide, Agile Procurement and Contracts

links.label: Agile Practice Guide, Agile Procurement and Contracts

q: Who should lead procurement negotiation, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: The project manager, since they know the scope best
The sponsor, because the sponsor funds the project
The vendor's account manager, who drafts the contract
A procurement team member with authority to sign
explanation: Negotiation should be led by a procurement team member with the authority to sign contracts. The project manager and the project management team may attend to assist.

q: The legal team wants to push a vendor into a win-lose contract. What should the project manager do?
options: Support the legal team, since winning saves money
Push for a win-win so both sides stay productive
Leave the contract terms entirely to the lawyers
Ask the vendor to sign its own boilerplate contract
explanation: The best long-term results come when both sides feel the contract is fair. A vendor that loses may do the bare minimum or send its least experienced people.
ref: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 9, Q4

links.label: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 9, Q4

q: Two weeks into a fixed-price contract, the vendor's lead asks the project manager to add a new report for free. The project manager has no contracting authority. What should they do?
options: Agree, to keep the vendor relationship friendly
Refer it to the procurement lead who holds authority
Promise extra money later if the report is added
Add the report to the scope baseline at once
explanation: Changes to rights and obligations are agreed through procurement, led by the person with authority to sign. The project manager assists but cannot commit the organization.

q: What should the project manager do first about the vendor's claim for the lab-system link?
options: Refer the claim to litigation to protect the hospital
Negotiate with the vendor, using the SOW and records
Stop all payments until the vendor drops the claim
Ask an arbitrator for a binding decision straight away
explanation: A contested change is a claim. Settling it through negotiation is the preferred method, supported by the contract terms and detailed project records. Arbitration and litigation come later, if negotiation fails.

q: The last two portal releases missed the response-time targets in the service-level agreement. Which tool checks the vendor's work against the agreement?
options: A bidder conference
A make-or-buy analysis
A performance review
A request for information
explanation: Performance reviews for contracts measure, compare and analyze quality, resource, schedule and cost performance against the agreement.

q: The hospital board asks whether this vendor may bid for the next project. Which record helps answer this?
options: Seller performance evaluation documentation
The minutes of the original bidder conference
The make-or-buy decision
The request for quote
explanation: The buyer prepares seller performance evaluation documentation: it rates how well the seller performed and whether it can work on future projects. Poor performers may be removed from the prequalified seller list.

q: Which THREE are characteristics of an integrated project delivery (IPD) contract?
options: A multiparty agreement with owner, designer and contractor
Shared risks and rewards based on project outcomes
Open-book accounting for financial transparency
Separate contracts with no shared incentives
Contractor involved only after the design is final
Award based only on the lowest bid
explanation: IPD contracts are used on complex construction projects. They involve all key parties early, share risks and rewards, use collaborative decisions and keep open-book accounting.

q: Which TWO must be true before a procurement is formally closed?
options: No claims or invoices are outstanding
All deliverables meet the technical and quality requirements
The seller has been added to the prequalified seller list
A new RFP has been issued for the next phase
An arbitration panel has reviewed the contract
explanation: Typically all deliverables are on time and meet the technical and quality requirements, no claims or invoices are outstanding, and final payments are made. The buyer then gives formal written notice that the contract is complete.

q: Match each dispute resolution method with how it works.
right: Direct talks between the parties, no third party
A neutral third party helps the parties agree
A panel hears both sides and makes a binding decision
A court decides, as the last option
explanation: Other methods are dispute review boards, appointed at the start of the project, and expert determination on one technical or financial issue.
